Exponential Modalities and Complementarity (extended abstract)
Robin Cockett Priyaa Varshinee Srinivasan

Abstract
The exponential modalities of linear logic have been used by various authors to model infinite-dimensional quantum systems. This paper explains how these modalities can also give rise to the complementarity principle of quantum mechanics. The paper uses a formulation of quantum systems based on † \dagger -linear logic, whose categorical semantics lies in mixed unitary categories, and a formulation of measurement therein. The main result exhibits a complementary system as the result of measurements on free exponential modalities. Recalling that, in linear logic, exponential modalities have two distinct but dual components, ! ! and ? ? , this shows how these components under measurement become “compacted” into the usual notion of a complementary Frobenius algebras from categorical quantum mechanics.



1
Introduction

Linear logic introduced by Girard in his seminal paper
[
18
]
treats logical statements
as resources, which cannot be duplicated or destroyed. The word “linear” refers to this
resource sensitivity of the logic: a proof of a statement in linear logic may thus be regarded as a series of
resource transformations. In full linear logic the classical ability to duplicate and destroy resources is
recaptured by the exponential (or storage) modality written
!
(pronounced the “bang”). The type
!A

may be interpreted as an unbounded “store” from which resources of type
A
can be extracted an arbitrary (including 0)
number of times.

The exponential modality
!
has been proposed as a structure for modelling infinite dimensional systems:
[
24
]
used the
exponential modality to model the quantum harmonic oscillator, and
[
6
]
used it to model the bosonic Fock space.
However, these uses did not explain what exponential modalities
!
and its dual
?
(pronounced the “whimper”)
have to do with the complementarity principle of quantum mechanics
[
12
]
. A pair of
quantum observables (physical properties of a system) is said to be complementary if
measuring one observable increases the uncertainty regarding the value of the other.
The classic example is that the more one knows about position of a particle the less one knows about its momentum.
The purpose of this article is to exhibit a relationship between the exponential modalities
!
and its dual
?
,
and complementary observables — a relationship which suggests a possibly new perspective on measurement in quantum systems.

Linearly distributive categories (LDCs)
[
9
]
provide a categorical semantics for the multiplicative fragment of linear logic (MLL).
Thus, LDCs are equipped with two distinct tensors called the “tensor”,
\otimes
, and the “par”,
\oplus
.
1
1

1

In the linear
logic community the par is often denoted by
\invamp
but we follow the convention in
[
9
]
and use
\oplus
.

These are related by a linear distributor. It is not assumed that the tensor is dual to the par — which would be normal in linear logic.
In an LDC, having a dual is a property which an object may or may not possess. When every object possesses a dual then the category is
*
-autonomous.

In this development, LDCs which satisfy the so-called “mix law” are particularly important. The mix law provides a natural transformation from
the tensor to the par called the
mixor
. When the mixor is a natural isomorphism the LDC becomes equivalent to a monoidal category.
Conversely, monoidal categories can be viewed as being degenerate or
compact
LDCs in which the mixor is the identity map.
Thus, from this perspective, a compact closed category is a compact LDC with duals, that is, a compact
*
-autonomous category.

In
[
7
]
, we introduced
\dagger
-linearly distributive categories (
\dagger
-LDCs) with mix for modelling possibly infinite-dimensional
quantum processes. In a mix LDC, there is always a set of objects which cannot distinguish between the tensor and the par in the sense
that
A\otimes\_\simeq A\oplus\_
: these objects form a compact subLDC called the
core
. In a mix
\dagger
-LDC, it is possible to go one
step further, and identify a
unitary core
in which every object is not only in the core but isomorphic to its
\dagger
-dual in a coherent way.
A unitary core is equivalent to a
\dagger
-monoidal category and when this category has duals it is equivalently a
\dagger
-compact closed
category
[
2
,
22
]
. This is the main structure underlying categorical quantum mechanics (CQM)
[
13
,
20
]
:
finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces provide the paradigmatic example.

The general notion of a
mixed unitary category
(MUC) is essentially a mix
\dagger
-LDC with a specified unitary core. In particular, the unitary core
may be viewed as comprising the finite-dimensional processes while the larger category extends this to include infinite-dimensional processes.
An example of a MUC is given by the embedding of complex finite matrices into the category of finiteness matrices
[
17
]
. Another example is given by
the embedding of the finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces within the category of
Chu spaces
[
3
]
of vector spaces over complex numbers
with the field
\mathbb{C}
as the dualizing object. For further details see
[
7
,
10
]
, where completely positive maps, and environment structures
for MUCs are described. In this article, we explore the notions of measurement and complementarity in MUCs.

In CQM, Coecke and Pavlovic
[
14
]
described a “demolition” measurement in a

\dagger
-monoidal category as a map,
m:A\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}X
, with

m^{\dagger}m=1_{X}
, to a special commutative
\dagger
-Frobenius algebra,
X
. Interpreted
in the category of finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces, the notion of the demolition measurement
models the Projection-Valued Measures (PVMs) of quantum mechanics.
Generalizing this idea to MUCs to model measurements here is complicated by the fact that, in a MUC,
generally,
A\neq A^{\dagger}
, except in the unitary core. Thus, in a MUC, a measurement can be viewed as a two-step process
in which one first “compacts” an object into the unitary core by a retraction and then one performs Coecke and Pavlovic’s
demolition measurement. The compaction process is discussed in Section
3
and is already quite interesting: it gives
rise to a
\dagger
-binary idempotent. Conversely, a
\dagger
-binary idempotent, which is “coring” and splits, gives rise to a compaction
into the “canonical” unitary core.

In CQM, quantum observables are characterized by certain
\dagger
-Frobenius algebras
[
15
]
in

\dagger
-monoidal categories. Two such
\dagger
-Frobenius algebras,

.

2
Preliminaries

In this section, we recall the definitions of dagger isomix categories, unitary categories, and
mixed unitary categories from
[
7
]
. To achieve this we start by recalling the definitions of linearly distributive
categories and isomix categories.

A linearly distributive category (LDC)
[
9
]
,
(\mathbb{X},\otimes,\oplus)
, is a category with two tensor products —
\otimes
called the tensor with
unit
\top
, and the
\oplus
called the par with unit
\bot
. The tensor and the par interact by means of
linear distributors which are natural transformations (which, in general, are not isomorphisms):

\partial^{L}:A\otimes(B\oplus C)\rightarrow(A\otimes B)\oplus C~~~~~~~~~~~~\partial^{R}:(B\oplus C)\otimes A\rightarrow B\oplus(C\otimes A)

A symmetric LDC is an LDC in which both monoidal structures are symmetric, with symmetry maps
c_{\otimes}:A\otimes B\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}B\otimes A
and
c_{\oplus}:A\oplus B\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}B\oplus A
, such that

\partial^{R}=c_{\otimes}(1\otimes c_{\oplus})\partial^{L}(c_{\otimes}\oplus 1)c_{\oplus}
.
LDCs provide a categorical semantics for linear logic, and are equipped with a graphical calculus; see
[
7
, Section 2]

and
[
5
]
.

A mix category is an LDC with a mix map,
{\sf m}:\bot\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\top
; when
{\sf m}
is an isomorphism it is an isomix category. The mix map gives a natural mixor map,

\mathsf{mx}:A\otimes B\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}A\oplus B
, which, even if the mix map is an isomorphism, is usually not an isomorphism. An isomix category in which every mixor map
is an isomorphism is a compact LDC. A compact LDC with
{\sf m}=1
and
\mathsf{mx}=1
is just a monoidal category.

The
core
,
\mathsf{Core}(\mathbb{X})
, of an isomix category
\mathbb{X}
is the full subcategory given by the objects,
U
,
such that for all
A\in\mathbb{X}
, the maps
\mathsf{mx}_{U,A}:U\otimes A\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}U\oplus A
and
\mathsf{mx}_{A,U}:A\otimes U\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}A\oplus U
are isomorphisms.
The units,
\top
and
\bot
, are always in the core. The core
\mathsf{Core}(\mathbb{X})
of an isomix category
\mathbb{X}
is always a compact LDC.

A
\dagger
-linearly distributive category

[
7
]
is an LDC
\mathbb{X}
with a functor
(\_)^{\dagger}:\mathbb{X}^{\mathsf{op}}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{X}
and the following natural isomorphisms satisfying the coherence conditions which are
described in
[
7
]
.

\displaystyle\text{ \bf tensor laxors: }A^{\dagger}\otimes B^{\dagger}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to21.05417pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$\lambda_{\otimes}$}}}(A\oplus B)^{\dagger}~~~~~~~~~~A^{\dagger}\oplus B^{\dagger}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to21.05417pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$\lambda_{\oplus}$}}}(A\otimes B)^{\dagger}

\displaystyle\text{ \bf unit laxors: }\top\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to21.05417pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$\lambda_{\top}$}}}\bot^{\dagger}~~~~~~~~~~~\bot\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to21.05417pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$\lambda_{\bot}$}}}\top^{\dagger}

\displaystyle\text{ \bf involutor: }A\xrightarrow{\iota}(A^{\dagger})^{\dagger}

In a
\dagger
-LDC, it is generally the case that
A\neq A^{\dagger}
because
\dagger
swaps the tensor and the par. A
\dagger
-mix category
is a
\dagger
-LDC which has a mix map which satisfies, in addition the following commuting diagram:

\mbox{\bf[$\dagger$-\text{mix}]}~~~~\begin{array}[c]{c}\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.5pt\hbox{\kern 16.6598pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\hbox{\vtop{\halign{\entry@#!@&&\entry@@#!@\cr&\cr&\crcr}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern-6.8889pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.5pt\hbox{$\textstyle{\bot\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 15.19167pt\raise 4.55556pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise-1.55556pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{{\sf m}}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 35.05556pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern-16.6598pt\raise-11.22179pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise-1.90001pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\lambda_{\bot}}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise-13.45357pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\kern 35.05556pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.5pt\hbox{$\textstyle{\top\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 41.94446pt\raise-11.22179pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise-1.90001pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\lambda_{\top}}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 41.94446pt\raise-13.45357pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\kern-8.97223pt\raise-22.44359pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.5pt\hbox{$\textstyle{\top^{\dagger}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 13.275pt\raise-28.6886pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise-3.24501pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{{\sf m}^{\dagger}}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 32.97223pt\raise-22.44359pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\kern 32.97223pt\raise-22.44359pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.5pt\hbox{$\textstyle{\bot^{\dagger}}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces}}}}\end{array}

If
{\sf m}
is an isomorphism, then
\mathbb{X}
is an
\dagger
-isomix category
. A
compact
\dagger
-LDC

is a compact LDC which is also a
\dagger
-isomix category.

In a
\dagger
-monoidal category a unitary isomorphism is an isomorphism
f
with
f^{\dagger}=f
.
In a
\dagger
-LDC, an object,
A
, does not necessarily coincide with its dagger,
A^{\dagger}
: this
means that describing unitary isomorphism for
\dagger
-LDCs is more complicated. To accomplish this
the notion of
unitary structure
which is described in
[
7
]
is used.
A
pre-unitary
object in a
\dagger
-isomix category is an object
A
in the core with an isomorphism

\varphi:A\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}A^{\dagger}
such that
\varphi(\varphi^{-1})^{\dagger}=\iota
(where
\iota
is the involutor). Unitary structure for a

\dagger
-isomix category is given by a family of pre-unitary objects satisfying certain closure and
coherences requirements.

A
unitary category
is a compact
\dagger
-LDC equipped with unitary structure which
makes every object a (pre)unitary object. A
\dagger
-monoidal category
[
20
]

is a unitary category with
\otimes=\oplus
and the unitary structure given by the
identity map. Conversely, every unitary category is
\dagger
-linearly equivalent to a

\dagger
-monoidal category via the
\dagger
-linear functor
{\sf Mx_{\downarrow}}:(\mathbb{X},\otimes,\oplus)\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}(\mathbb{X},\otimes,\otimes)
,
see
[
7
, Prop. 5.11]
.

A
mixed unitary category
(MUC)
[
7
]
is a
\dagger
-isomix category,
\mathbb{C}
,
equipped with a strong
\dagger
-isomix functor
M:\mathbb{U}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{C}
from a unitary category

\mathbb{U}
such that there are natural transformations:

\mathsf{mx}^{\prime}:M(U)\otimes X\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}M(U)\oplus X\text{ with }\mathsf{mx}~\mathsf{mx}^{\prime}=1,~\mathsf{mx}^{\prime}\mathsf{mx}=1

Thus, a mixed unitary category can be visualized schematically as:

A\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to21.43474pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$\varphi_{A}$}}_{\hbox{\scriptsize$\simeq$}}}A^{\dagger}
Unitary
category
\dagger
-isomix
functor
\dagger
-isomix
category
B
B^{\dagger}
\mathsf{Core}

Within the unitary category,
A\simeq A^{\dagger}
by the means of the unitary structure map.
However, outside the unitary core, an object is not in general isomorphic to its dagger.

Given any
\dagger
-isomix category
\mathbb{X}
, the preunitary objects always
form a unitary category,
\mathsf{Unitary}(\mathbb{X})
with a forgetful
\dagger
-isomix functor
U:\mathsf{Unitary}(\mathbb{X})\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{X}

which produces a MUC.
\mathsf{Unitary}(\mathbb{X})
satisfies a couniversal property, see
[
7
, Section 5.2]
,
and is the “largest” possible unitary core for the
\dagger
-isomix category
\mathbb{X}
. We shall call

\mathsf{Unitary}(\mathbb{X})
the
canonical
unitary core of
\mathbb{X}
.

3
Measurement

A measurement in a MUC can be broken into two steps: a compaction step into an object in the unitary core followed by
a demolition measurement within the unitary core.

Definition 3.1
.

Let
M:\mathbb{U}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{C}
be a MUC. A
compaction
of an object
A\in\mathbb{C}
to
U\in\mathbb{U}
is a retraction,

r:A\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}M(U)
. This means that there is a section
s:M(U)\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}A
such that
sr=1_{M(U)}
.
A compaction is said to be
canonical
when
\mathbb{U}=\mathsf{Unitary}(\mathbb{X})
(so
U
is a preunitary object).

The compact object,
M(U)
, has a unitary structure map which is an isomorphism between
M(U)

and
M(U)^{\dagger}
given by composing the unitary structure map of
U
with the preservator
\rho
(see
[
7
, Definition 3.17]
for the complete definiton of a preservator):

\psi:=M(U)\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to31.88617pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$M(\varphi)$}}}M(U^{\dagger})\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to16.14897pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$\rho$}}}M(U)^{\dagger}

Once one has reached
M(U)
by a compaction, one can follow with a classical demolition measurement
U\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to17.97339pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$w$}}}X
to obtain an overall
compaction
A\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to36.52808pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$rM(w)$}}}M(X)
, which gives a (demolition) measurement in a MUC.

We start by showing how a compaction gives rise to a binary idempotent:

Definition 3.2
.

A
binary idempotent
in any category is a pair of maps
({\sf{u}},{\sf{v}})
with
{\sf{u}}:A\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}B
, and
{\sf{v}}:B\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}A
such that
{\sf{u}}{\sf{v}}{\sf{u}}={\sf{u}}
, and
{\sf{v}}{\sf{u}}{\sf{v}}={\sf{v}}
.

A binary idempotent,
({\sf{u}},{\sf{v}}):A\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}B
gives a pair of idempotents:
e_{A}:={\sf{u}}{\sf{v}}:A\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}A
, and
e_{B}:={\sf{v}}{\sf{u}}:B\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}B
.
We say the binary idempotent
({\sf{u}},{\sf{v}})

splits
in case the idempotents
e_{A}
and
e_{B}
split.

Lemma 3.3
.

In any category the following are equivalent:

(i)

({\sf{u}},{\sf{v}}):A\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}B
is a binary idempotent which splits.

(ii)

e:A\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}A
, and
d:B\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}B
are a pair of idempotents which split through isomorphic objects.

Observe that a compaction of an object, say
A
, in any MUC, gives the following system of maps:

\textstyle{A\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{r}
\textstyle{M(U)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{s}
\scriptstyle{\psi:=M(\varphi)\rho}
\textstyle{M(U)^{\dagger}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{r^{\dagger}}
\scriptstyle{\psi^{-1}}
\textstyle{A^{\dagger}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{s^{\dagger}}

Thus the compaction gives rise to a binary idempotent
({\sf{u}},{\sf{v}}):A\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}A^{\dagger}

where
{\sf{u}}:=r\psi r^{\dagger}
and
{\sf{v}}:=s^{\dagger}\psi^{-1}s
.

Because
U
is a unitary object, we have that
\varphi(\varphi^{-1\dagger})=\iota
.
The preservator, on the other hand, satisfies
\iota\rho^{\dagger}=M(\iota)\rho

(see after Definition 3.17 in
[
7
]
). Thus,
\iota\rho^{\dagger}=M(\iota)\rho=M(\varphi\varphi^{-1\dagger})\rho=M(\varphi)\rho M(\varphi^{-1})^{\dagger}
and hence

\psi=M(\varphi)\rho=\iota\rho^{\dagger}M(\varphi)^{\dagger}=\iota(M(\varphi)\rho)^{\dagger}=\iota\psi^{\dagger}
.
This allows us to observe:

\displaystyle\iota{\sf{u}}^{\dagger}

\displaystyle=\iota(r\psi r^{\dagger})^{\dagger}=\iota r^{\dagger\dagger}\psi^{\dagger}r^{\dagger}=r\iota\psi^{\dagger}r^{\dagger}=r\psi r^{\dagger}={\sf{u}}

\displaystyle{\sf{v}}^{\dagger}

\displaystyle=(s^{\dagger}\psi^{-1}s)^{\dagger}=s^{\dagger}(\psi^{\dagger})^{-1}s^{\dagger\dagger}=s^{\dagger}(\iota^{-1}\psi)^{-1}s^{\dagger\dagger}=s^{\dagger}\psi^{-1}\iota s^{\dagger\dagger}=s^{\dagger}\psi^{-1}s\iota={\sf{v}}\iota

This leads to the following definition:

Definition 3.4
.

A binary idempotent,
({\sf{u}},{\sf{v}}):A\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}A^{\dagger}
in a
\dagger
-LDC is a
\dagger
-binary idempotent
,
written
\dagger({\sf{u}},{\sf{v}})
, if
{\sf{u}}=\iota{\sf{u}}^{\dagger}

and
{\sf{v}}^{\dagger}={\sf{v}}\iota
.

In a
\dagger
-monoidal category, where
A=A^{\dagger}
and
\iota=1_{A}

this makes
{\sf{u}}={\sf{u}}^{\dagger}
and
{\sf{v}}={\sf{v}}^{\dagger}
; thus
{\sf{u}}{\sf{v}}=({\sf{v}}{\sf{u}})^{\dagger}
. This means
that if we require
{\sf{u}}{\sf{v}}={\sf{v}}{\sf{u}}
we obtain a dagger idempotent in the sense of
[
23
]
.

Splitting a
\dagger
-binary idempotent almost produces a preunitary object. In a
\dagger
-LDC, we shall call an object
A

with an isomorphism
\varphi:A\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}A^{\dagger}
such that
\varphi\varphi^{\dagger-1}=\iota
a
weak preunitary object
.
Clearly, in a
\dagger
-isomix category, a weak preunitary object
(A,\varphi)
is a preunitary object when, in addition,

A
is in the core. We next observe that dagger binary idempotent splits through weak preunitary objects:

Lemma 3.5
.

In a
\dagger
-LDC with a
\dagger
-binary idempotent
\dagger({\sf{u}},v):A\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}A^{\dagger}
:

(i)

e_{A^{\dagger}}:={\sf{v}}{\sf{u}}=({\sf{u}}{\sf{v}})^{\dagger}=:(e_{A})^{\dagger}
;

(ii)

if
\dagger({\sf{u}},{\sf{v}})
splits with
e_{A}=A\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to15.92824pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$r$}}}E\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to15.7743pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$s$}}}A
then
E
is a weak preunitary object.

Thus, in a
\dagger
-isomix category, an object which splits a
\dagger
-binary idempotent is always weakly preunitary.
In order to ensure that the splitting of a
\dagger
-binary idempotent is a preunitary object — and so a canonical compaction — it
remains to ensure that the splitting is in the core. This leads to the following definition:

Definition 3.6
.

An idempotent
A\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to15.7941pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$e$}}}A
in an isomix category,
\mathbb{X}
, is a
coring idempotent
if it is equipped with natural

\kappa^{L}_{X}:X\oplus A\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}X\otimes A
and
\kappa^{R}_{X}:A\oplus X\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}A\otimes X
such that the following diagrams
commute:

\textstyle{X\otimes A\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{1\otimes e}
\scriptstyle{1\otimes e}
\scriptstyle{\bf[KL.1]}
\textstyle{X\otimes A\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\mathsf{mx}}
\textstyle{X\otimes A}
\textstyle{X\oplus A\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\kappa^{L}_{X}}

\textstyle{X\oplus A\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{1\oplus e}
\scriptstyle{1\oplus e}
\scriptstyle{\bf[KL.2]}
\textstyle{X\oplus A\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\kappa^{L}_{X}}
\textstyle{X\oplus A}
\textstyle{X\otimes A\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\mathsf{mx}}

\textstyle{A\otimes X\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{e\otimes 1}
\scriptstyle{e\otimes 1}
\scriptstyle{\bf[KR.1]}
\textstyle{A\otimes X\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\mathsf{mx}}
\textstyle{A\otimes X}
\textstyle{A\oplus X\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\kappa^{R}_{X}}

\textstyle{A\oplus X\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{e\oplus 1}
\scriptstyle{e\oplus 1}
\scriptstyle{\bf[KR.2]}
\textstyle{A\oplus X\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\kappa^{R}_{X}}
\textstyle{A\oplus X}
\textstyle{A\otimes X\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\mathsf{mx}}

For a coring idempotent
A\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to15.7941pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$e$}}}A
, the transformations
\kappa^{\_}_{X}
act on a splitting as the inverse of the mixor,
\mathsf{mx}
. Thus, a coring idempotent
always splits through the core:

Lemma 3.7
.

In a mix category:

(i)

An idempotent splits through the core if and only if it is coring;

(ii)

If
(u,v)
is a binary idempotent then
{\sf{u}}{\sf{v}}
is coring if and only if
{\sf{v}}{\sf{u}}
is coring.

This allows:

Definition 3.8
.

A
coring binary idempotent
in a mix category is a binary idempotent,
({\sf{u}},{\sf{v}})
, for which either
{\sf{u}}{\sf{v}}
or
{\sf{v}}{\sf{u}}

is a coring idempotent.

These observations can be summarized by the following:

Theorem 3.9
.

In the MUC
M\!:\!\mathsf{Unitary}(\mathbb{X})\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{X}
, with
\dagger
-isomix category
\mathbb{X}
, an object
U
is a compaction of
A
if and only if
U
is the
splitting of a coring
\dagger
-binary idempotent
\dagger({\sf{u}},{\sf{v}}):A\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}A^{\dagger}
.

Using this characterization of canonical compaction, we will show that, in the presence of free
\dagger
-exponential
modalities, complementarity always arises as a canonical compaction of a
\dagger
-linear bialgebra on
the free exponential modalities.

4
Complementarity

The objective of this section, is to describe strong complementarity within a
\dagger
-isomix category. Strong complementarity
classically is, in a
\dagger
-monoidal setting, between two special commutative
\dagger
-Frobenius algebras.
In a linear setting with two distinct tensor products, Frobenius Algebras are generalized by linear monoids
[
16
,
8
]

which consist of a
\otimes
-monoid and a dual
\oplus
-comonoid. The directionality of the linear distributor makes a bialgebraic interaction between two

\dagger
-linear monoids impossible. However, such an interaction is possible between a

\dagger
-linear monoid and a
\dagger
-linear comonoid, and this gives a
\dagger
-linear bialgebra. These
\dagger
-linear bialgebras provide the basis for complementarity in a
\dagger
-isomix category.
In a MUC, one can, furthermore, consider the effect of a compaction which preserves these structures to arrive back at the classical CQM notion
of a complementary system.

4.1
Duals

Definition 4.1
.

A
dual
in an LDC,
(\eta,\epsilon):A\dashv\!\!\!\!\!\dashv B
, consists of maps,

\eta:\top\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}A\oplus B
, and
\epsilon:B\otimes A\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\bot
such that the
snake diagrams hold. A
morphism of duals
,
(f,g):(\eta,\epsilon):A\dashv\!\!\!\!\!\dashv B\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}(\tau,\gamma):A^{\prime}\dashv\!\!\!\!\!\dashv B^{\prime}
, is given by a pair of maps

f:A\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}A^{\prime}
and
g:B^{\prime}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}B
such that:

(a)
\tau
A^{\prime}
B^{\prime}
g
B

=
\eta
B
A
f
A^{\prime}

(b)
\gamma
B^{\prime}
A^{\prime}
f
A

=
\epsilon
A
B
g
B^{\prime}

A
self-duality
is a dual
(\eta,\epsilon):A\dashv\!\!\!\!\!\dashv B
in which
A
is isomorphic to
B
(or indeed
A=B
).

A morphism
(f,g)
of duals is determined by either of the maps, as
f
is
dual to
g
: they are Australian mates; see
[
8
]
.
In a
\dagger
-LDC, if
A
is dual to
B
, then
B^{\dagger}
is dual to
A^{\dagger}
:

A binary idempotent can implicitly express a morphism of duals, which becomes explicit when the idempotent splits.

Definition 4.2
.

A binary idempotent
({\sf{u}},{\sf{v}})
is
retractional
on a dual
(\eta,\epsilon):A\dashv\!\!\!\!\!\dashv B
if equations
(a)
and
(b)
, below, hold.
On the other hand
({\sf{u}},{\sf{v}})
is
sectional
, if equations
(c)
and
(d)
hold:

(a)~\hbox to31.35pt{\vbox to32.8pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 76.06348pt\lower 3.3066pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \hbox to0.0pt{

where
e_{A}:={\sf{u}}{\sf{v}}
and
e_{B}:={\sf{v}}{\sf{u}}
.

The idempotent pair
(e_{A},e_{B})
is a morphism of duals only when the binary idempotent is both sectional and retractional.

Lemma 4.3
.

In an LDC, a binary idempotent
({\sf{u}},{\sf{v}})
on a dual
(\eta,\epsilon):A\dashv\!\!\!\!\!\dashv B
,
with splitting
A\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to15.92824pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$r$}}}E\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to15.7743pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$s$}}}
A and
B\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to17.77573pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$r^{\prime}$}}}E^{\prime}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to17.6218pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$s^{\prime}$}}}B
is sectional (respectively retractional) if and only if the
section
(s,r^{\prime})
(respectively the retraction
(r,s^{\prime})
) is a morphism for
(\eta(r\oplus r^{\prime}),(s^{\prime}\otimes s)\epsilon):E\dashv\!\!\!\!\!\dashv E^{\prime}
.

Splitting binary idempotents which are either sectional or retractional on a dual produces a self-duality.

We next observe that the dagger of a dual is itself a dual:

Lemma 4.4
.

Suppose
\mathbb{X}
is a
\dagger
-LDC, and
(\eta,\epsilon):A\dashv\!\!\!\!\!\dashv B
is a dual in
\mathbb{X}
.
Then,
(\epsilon\dagger,\eta\dagger):B^{\dagger}\dashv\!\!\!\!\!\dashv A^{\dagger}
is a dual where:

\displaystyle\epsilon\dagger

\displaystyle:=\top\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to21.05417pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$\lambda_{\top}$}}}\bot^{\dagger}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to18.01076pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$\epsilon^{\dagger}$}}}(B\otimes A)^{\dagger}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to21.32639pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$\lambda_{\oplus}^{-1}$}}}B^{\dagger}\oplus A^{\dagger}

\displaystyle\eta\dagger

\displaystyle:=A^{\dagger}\otimes B^{\dagger}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to21.05417pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$\lambda_{\otimes}$}}}(A\oplus B)^{\dagger}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to18.79794pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$\eta^{\dagger}$}}}\top^{\dagger}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to21.32639pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$\lambda_{\bot}^{-1}$}}}\bot

4.2
Linear monoid

The simplest way to describe a linear monoid is as a
\otimes
-monoid on an object together
with a dual for that object. Their similarity to Frobenius algebras becomes more apparent when one regards
a linear monoid as a
\otimes
-monoid and a
\oplus
-comonoid with actions and coactions.

(4.6.1)

In a symmetric LDC, a linear monoid is
symmetric
when its duals are symmetric, i.e,
\eta_{R}=\eta_{L}c_{\oplus}
and

\epsilon_{R}=c_{\otimes}\epsilon_{L}
. A symmetric linear monoid is determined by a monoid
(A,m,u)
and a dual
(\eta,\epsilon):A\dashv\!\!\!\!\!\dashv B
.
There is a more useful form for linear monoids in which their similarity to the usual description of Frobenius algebras in CQM is evident:

Proposition 4.7
.

In a linear bicategory, the structure described in Proposition
4.7

is called a linear monad
[
8
]
: here, as we are in a
simpler context, we use linear monoid. A linear monoid
A\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.5pt\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\hbox{\vtop{\halign{\entry@#!@&&\entry@@#!@\cr&\crcr}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern-3.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.5pt\hbox{$\textstyle{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 3.64192pt\raise 4.62848pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise-1.62848pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\circ}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.38109pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern-2.0pt\lower 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@stopper}}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\lower 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@stopper}}\hbox{}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\kern 14.38109pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.5pt\hbox{$\textstyle{}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces}}}}\ignorespaces B
,
in a monoidal category gives a Frobenius algebra when it is a self-linear monoid that is
A=B
and the duality coincide with the self-dual cup and cap.
Note that
while a Frobenius algebra is always on a self-dual object, a linear monoid allows Frobenius interaction
between distinct objects which are duals of one another.

Definition 4.8
.

A
morphism of linear monoids
is a pair of maps,
(f,g):(A\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\hbox{\vtop{\halign{\entry@#!@&&\entry@@#!@\cr&\crcr}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern-3.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.55554pt\hbox{$\textstyle{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 3.64192pt\raise 4.62848pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise-1.62848pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\circ}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.38109pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern-2.0pt\lower 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@stopper}}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\lower 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@stopper}}\hbox{}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\kern 14.38109pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.55554pt\hbox{$\textstyle{}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces}}}}\ignorespaces B)\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}(A^{\prime}\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\hbox{\vtop{\halign{\entry@#!@&&\entry@@#!@\cr&\crcr}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern-3.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.55554pt\hbox{$\textstyle{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 3.64192pt\raise 4.62848pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise-1.62848pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\circ}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.38109pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern-2.0pt\lower 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@stopper}}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\lower 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@stopper}}\hbox{}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\kern 14.38109pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.55554pt\hbox{$\textstyle{}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces}}}}\ignorespaces B^{\prime})
, such that

f:A\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}A^{\prime}
is a monoid morphism (or equivalently
g:B^{\prime}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}B
is a comonoid morphism),
and
(f,g)
and
(g,f)
preserve the left and the right duals respectively.

Note that a morphism of Frobenius algebras is usually given by a single monoid morphism
which is an isomorphism. However, in the case of a morphism of linear monoids,
the comonoid morphism,
g:B^{\prime}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}B
, is the cyclic mate of the monoid morphism,
f:A\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}A^{\prime}
.
This means that a linear monoid morphism is not restricted to being an isomorphism.

Given an idempotent
e_{A}:A\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}A
, and a monoid
(A,m,u)
in a monoidal category,
e_{A}
is

retractional
on the monoid if
e_{A}m=e_{A}m(e_{A}\otimes e_{A})
.
e_{A}
is

sectional
on the monoid if
m(e_{A}\otimes e_{A})=e_{A}m(e_{A}\otimes e_{A})
and
ue_{A}=u
.

Lemma 4.9
.

In a monoidal category, a split idempotent
e:A\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}A
on a monoid
(A,m,u)
,
with splitting
A\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to15.92824pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$r$}}}E\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to15.7743pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$s$}}}
A, is sectional (respectively retractional) if and only if the
section
s
(respectively the retraction
r
) is a monoid morphism for
(E,(s\otimes s)mr,ur)
.

Splitting a sectional/retractional binary idempotent on a linear monoid gives a self-linear monoid on the splitting.

(4.10.1)

A
morphism
of
\dagger
-linear monoids is a pair of maps
(f,f^{\dagger})
which are
morphisms of underlying linear monoids.
Similar to duals, splitting sectional/retractional binary idempotents on a linear monoid induces a
self-linear monoid. In the presence of dagger, one gets a
\dagger
-self-linear monoid

[
11
, Lemma 5.8]
.

A
\dagger
-linear monoid in a unitary category is equivalent to a
\dagger
-Frobenius algebra under certain conditions:

.

(4.11.1)

The equation in the previous Lemma reminds us of involutive
monoids

, Theorem 5.28]
in

-monoidal categories.

One can get Frobenius algebras by splitting binary idempotents on linear monoids:

Lemma 4.12
.

\mathbb{X}

(4.12.1)

and

.

In a
\dagger
-isomix category, splitting a sectional or retractional
\dagger
-coring binary idempotent
on a
\dagger
-linear monoid gives a
\dagger
-self-linear monoid on a pre-unitary object.
If the binary idempotent satisfies equation
4.12.1
, then, by using
Lemmas
4.11
and
4.12
, one
gets a
\dagger
-Frobenius algebra on the splitting.

4.3
Linear comonoid

The bialgebra law is a central ingredient of a complimentary system. The directionality of the linear distributors in an LDC
forbids a bialgebraic interaction between two linear monoids. A linear monoid, however, can interact bialgebraically
with a linear comonoid.

.

(4.13.1)

Note that while a linear monoid has a
\otimes
-monoid and a
\oplus
-comonoid, a linear comonoid has a
\otimes
-comonoid and an
\oplus
-monoid.

A
morphism
of linear comonoids,

, consists of a pair of maps,

, such that

are morphisms of

In a monoidal category, an idempotent
e:A\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}A

is
sectional
(respectively
retractional
) on a comonoid
(A,d,k)

if
ed=ed(e\otimes e)
(respectively if
d(e\otimes e)=ed(e\otimes e)
and
ek=k
).
In an LDC, a binary idempotent
({\sf{u}},{\sf{v}})
is
sectional
(respectively
retractional
) on a linear monoid when

e_{A}={\sf{u}}{\sf{v}}
and
e_{B}={\sf{v}}{\sf{u}}
satisfies the conditions in the table below.

(
u
,
v
)
sectional
on
A\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.5pt\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\hbox{\vtop{\halign{\entry@#!@&&\entry@@#!@\cr&\crcr}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern-3.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.5pt\hbox{$\textstyle{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 3.64192pt\raise-4.62846pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise-1.62848pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\circ}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.38109pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern-2.0pt\lower 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@stopper}}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\lower 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@stopper}}\hbox{}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\kern 14.38109pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.5pt\hbox{$\textstyle{}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces}}}}\ignorespaces B

({\sf{u}},{\sf{v}})

retractional
on
A\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.5pt\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\hbox{\vtop{\halign{\entry@#!@&&\entry@@#!@\cr&\crcr}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern-3.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.5pt\hbox{$\textstyle{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 3.64192pt\raise-4.62846pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise-1.62848pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\circ}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.38109pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern-2.0pt\lower 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@stopper}}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\lower 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@stopper}}\hbox{}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\kern 14.38109pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.5pt\hbox{$\textstyle{}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces}}}}\ignorespaces B

Splitting a sectional or retractional binary idempotent on a linear comonoid gives a self-linear comonoid.

Definition 4.14
.

A

(4.14.1)

A
\dagger
-self-linear comonoid
consists of an
isomorphism
\alpha:A\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}A^{\dagger}
such that
\alpha\alpha^{-1\dagger}=\iota
.
A
morphism of
\dagger
-linear comonoids
is a
pair
(f,f^{\dagger})
such that
(f,f^{\dagger})
is a morphism of the
underlying linear comonoids.

In a
\dagger
-LDC, splitting a
\dagger
-binary idempotent on a
\dagger
-linear comonoid
gives a
\dagger
-self-linear comonoid when the binary idempotent is either sectional or retractional.
In the next section, we discuss linear bialgebras which are given by an interacting linear monoid and linear comonoid.

4.4
Linear bialgebras

All the results concerning bialgebras are necessarily set in symmetric LDCs and we shall assume that linear monoids
and the linear comonoids are symmetric.

are
\otimes

A
morphism
of linear bialgebras is a morphism both of the linear monoids and linear comonoids.

A linear bialgebra is
commutative
if the
\oplus
-monoid and
\otimes
-monoid are commutative.
A
self-linear bialgebra
is a linear bialgebra in which there is an isomorphism
A\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to17.19875pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$\alpha$}}}B

(so essentially the algebra is on one object).

A binary idempotent on a linear bialgebra is
sectional
(respectively
retractional
) if it is sectional (respectively retractional)
on the linear monoid, and the linear comonoid. In an LDC, splitting a sectional or retractional binary idempotent on a linear bialgebra induces a
self-linear bialgebra on the splitting.

\alpha:A\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}A^{\dagger}
, satisfies
\alpha\alpha^{-1\dagger}=\iota
.

Note that
A
is a weak preunitary object: if it was in the core as well, it would be a preunitary object.
In a
\dagger
-LDC, splitting a
\dagger
-binary idempotent on a
\dagger
-linear bialgebra gives a

\dagger
-self-linear bialgebra if the idempotent is either a sectional or retractional.

4.5
Complementary systems

In quantum mechanics, two quantum observables are complementary
[
19
]
if measuring one observable increases
the uncertainty regarding the value of the other. Complementarity is a key feature distinguishing classical from quantum mechanics.
In CQM, the complimentarity principle is described using interacting commutative
\dagger
-Frobenius algebras. This section describes complementarity in isomix categories:

Definition 4.17
.

A
complementary system
in an isomix category,
\mathbb{X}
, is a commutative and cocommutative
self-linear bialgebra,

A
\dagger
-complementary system
in a
\dagger
-isomix category is a
\dagger
-self-linear bialgebra which
is also a complementary system.

Notice that we are using the alternative presentation of linear monoids by actions and coactions (see
Proposition
4.7
). Thus,
[comp.1]
requires that the counit of the linear comonoid to be
dual to the counit via the linear monoid dual, while
[comp.2]
requires that the unit of the linear monoid to be dual to the
counit via dual of the linear comonoid. Finally,
[comp.3]
requires that the coaction map of the linear monoid
duplicates the unit of
\dagger
-linear comonoid. The ‘co’ symmetry of the equations are immediate
from the commutativity and cocommutativity of the linear bialgebra. The ‘op’ symmetry of equations
holds automatically for a
\dagger
-complimentary system.

The universal property of free exponential modalities in a
(!,?)
-LDC implies the following:

Lemma 5.2
.

If
(f,g)
is a morphism of duals, then the unique map
(f^{\flat},g^{\sharp})
induced by the
universal property of the free exponential is a morphism of linear comonoids.

.

6
Conclusion

Bohr’s principle of complementarity
[
19
]
states that, due to the wave and particle nature of matter, physical properties occur in
complimentary pairs. In the formulation of measurements in a MUC, a measurement on
A

induces a measurement on
A^{\dagger}
, and vice versa. A measurement transfers the structures of
A
and
A^{\dagger}
—
and the interactions between these — onto a single compact object. Our main result displays a complementary system
as the result of a measurement of a
\dagger
-linear bialgebra in which two distinct dual structures have been “compacted” into one structure.
This provides an interesting perspective on Bohr’s principle.
